speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I declare, Sir, my interest as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second cut, Sir, is on supporting small law firms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Ministry of Law's (MinLaw’s) work, as Members will know, touches on a number of aspects.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This includes maintaining a legal system that is robust, fair and effective; enhancing access to justice; and supporting our economic and social vibrancy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have made good progress and we intend to do more.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will focus on two areas: one, how can we help the vulnerable better get help when they deal with the criminal and civil law systems; and two, how can we better help resolve family law disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleagues, Minister Edwin Tong and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will touch on the other key areas in MinLaw’s work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, on access to the criminal and civil law systems, we are focused on ensuring access to justice, especially for the most vulnerable in our community.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this context, the Public Defender’s Office (PDO) and the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) have been doing good work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: PDO helps to facilitate access to justice for accused persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was set up in December 2022, as a department within MinLaw, to institutionalise public defence within our criminal justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Before that, the Government funded access to criminal defence via the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS), which was run by the Law Society.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Derrick Goh asked for updates on PDO’s work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of these, almost half were assessed as eligible for criminal defence aid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With our ongoing partnership with Pro Bono SG, eligible applicants receive representation from either PDO or from criminal lawyers working with CLAS.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As pointed out by Mr Goh, the complexity and impact of PDO cases go beyond legal matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He is married with two young children with special needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He meets with their teachers, attends their speech therapy classes and follow-ups at the hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: His wife is not actively involved in the caregiving.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He needed money urgently to cover daily living expenses and his children’s therapy sessions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He borrowed $1,000 from an unlicensed moneylender and he was subsequently harassed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He felt he had no choice but to assist the unlicensed moneylender in its illegal operations and he was subsequently charged for doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to take a serious view of this because that then potentially leads to scams and people losing lots of money, including the elderly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you want to prevent all of that, you need to take tough steps and draw a line when people assist illegal moneylenders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prior to these charges, he had a clean record.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr N could have expected a sentence of around eight to 12 months’ imprisonment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This would have meant that his children with special needs would be left without care during Mr N’s prison term.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Public Defender explained his situation to the Prosecution, and also pleaded with the Court for a lighter sentence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Public Defender also referred Mr N to a social service agency to assess the care plan for his children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court also agreed to defer his sentence, to allow Mr N to ease his child’s transition into Primary 1 at a special needs school.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will add that Mr N recently surrendered himself to the Court and he will serve his sentence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is one of many examples where PDO has positively impacted the lives of accused persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will continue to strengthen PDO, its capability and capacity to help more vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Moving to civil legal aid, last year was LAB’s 65th year of providing legal aid, assistance and advice to the less privileged.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was set up in 1958, started out as a small team of 15 staff to provide legal aid to needy persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, it is a department with about 50 in-house lawyers, support staff, as well as 140 Assigned Solicitors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are lawyers from private practice who work with LAB.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: LAB helps with various civil matters, including matrimonial matters, monetary claims and probate matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the years, it has helped many people.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, I will give you one example of a 101-year-old lady.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: LAB helped her to reclaim her life savings from her own daughter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This old lady spoke no English, only Hokkien.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She had been put in a nursing home by her daughter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Her daughter began withdrawing monies from the old lady’s bank account and directed the applicant’s Government financial assistance payouts to her, meaning the daughter’s own bank account.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Her daughter alleged that the applicant had no mental capacity and refused to return the monies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The applicant, the old lady, checked herself out of her nursing home and asked LAB for help.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To ensure that aid is provided to those who cannot afford a lawyer, we require applicants for aid to undergo means testing, and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will speak about the means assessment of our legal aid and criminal defence aid schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are also other possible mechanisms to increase access to justice besides Government legal aid and assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One of them is conditional fee agreements (CFAs).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we refer to Mr Zhulkarnain’s question on whether we will extend CFAs to other categories of proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach is, as far as possible, we will see what other means there are available to allow access to justice in an easier way and then study the applicability of CFAs, the usefulness of CFAs, the positive and negative consequences, by extending to other domestic litigation proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will move now to the second part of my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have invested considerable time, energy and resources to streamline and help people in the family justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where families have breakdowns, their relationships fray, they go to Court, we want to try and minimise the pain for those who have to be involved in the legal process.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The disputes often involve a lot of emotions, psychological wounds and children are often caught in the crossfire.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is why for some time now, we have taken a different approach from the usual litigation process.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For family cases, our Courts focus on therapeutic justice, which is about getting parties to establish common ground and move on with their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The changes we have made, over the years, to the family justice system reflect this approach, this philosophy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Ms Hany Soh referred, a major review was done in 2013, which resulted in amongst other things, the establishment of the Family Justice Courts (FJC).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Specialised FJC with specialised judges, with its own head of the FJC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Measures were introduced in divorce cases to help these cases proceed more smoothly and reduce animosity as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the focus was also on seeking to protect the children's welfare.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One very important measure is the simplified divorce track.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those on this track, it saves a lot of time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The divorce proceedings are concluded within a much shorter timeframe and is available to all parties who agree on the divorce and ancillary matters at the outset and, you can imagine, it helps to reduce acrimony.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is an incentive for parties to come to an agreement on the issues.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of that, more than 4,000 – to be precise, around 4,150 or 66% of divorce cases – went on the simplified track and almost half of these cases involved children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can imagine if these 4,000 cases were handled under the normal litigation process.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amount of time, the money, the acrimony and the impact on the children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, all of that has been considerably reduced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is a significant number of couples, over 4,000 couples, their children, who we hope were better able to move on with their lives with as little acrimony as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is much quicker, much less costly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where the divorce or ancillary matters are contested, FJC offers free in-house mediation and counselling, if certain criteria are met.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Around 930 out of 1,060 cases that went through mediation were fully or partially settled.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In September 2019, we set up a second Committee co-chaired by MinLaw, the Ministry for Social and Family Development (MSF) and FJC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And a slew of further recommendations were made to strengthen the therapeutic justice elements and address some of the challenges in the new family justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The recommendations of this new Committee have been progressively implemented: the Women's Charter was amended last year; MinLaw's and MSF's Family Justice Reform Act was passed last year; and a number of other non-legislative initiatives have been undertaken by MSF and FJC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One of the key issues that the Family Justice Reform Act addressed, is the enforcement of maintenance orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We observed a fairly high incidence of non-compliance with maintenance orders and a significant number of repeat applications for enforcement, usually by the ex-wife applying repeatedly to enforce the maintenance orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Family Justice Reform Act introduced a new Maintenance Enforcement Process (MEP) which would help to address these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Under the MEP, there is a new unit of officers called Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MEOs will be empowered to obtain information about the parties' financial circumstances directly from the parties or from third-parties, such as banks and Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will relieve applicants from having to go around, instruct lawyers to apply to Court to get the information, that takes time, effort and cost – and usually, there is also non-compliance.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, when the respondent is non-cooperative, it can go on and on for months, sometimes years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With more accurate and clear information, the MEO and the Courts will be better able to distinguish between respondents who cannot pay and respondents who refuse to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those who refuse to pay, the system, the MEP, strengthens the deterrence against them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This system should hopefully help reduce repeated defaulters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Hany Soh asked about the implementation of the Family Justice Reform Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The other reforms will be implemented in stages.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Soh also asked about collaborations with stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Between us, we have regular conversations with the family bar, counsellors, mental health experts and community partners about how best to support families in distress.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also conduct regular outreach to various segments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I ask the public to share about family justice initiatives and therapeutic justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we can say, the situation has vastly improved since these amendments were put in place for some time now.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chairman, to sum up, we have been building steadily on our progress over the last few years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have taken significant steps and will continue to work on helping the vulnerable through the criminal and civil law systems; and enhancing dispute resolution in family disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Much of our growth depends on our ability to develop strong enterprises and attract foreign investments into Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, Singapore continues to be the partner of choice for many businesses – from the world's multinational corporations to the fastest growing startups.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have the highest number of regional headquarters in Asia Pacific.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: About 4,200 multinational companies (MNCs) host their regional headquarters here, using Singapore as the gateway into ASEAN, Asia and even the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have a vibrant innovation ecosystem with research and development labs for leading Fortune 500 companies; as well as over 150 venture capital funds, incubators and accelerators.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Businesses come here in large part because of our strong rule of law, trusted legal system, under-pinned by a well-respected Judiciary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They trust that their investments will be safe and that their rights will be protected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Businesses also work out of Singapore because they can access the best legal services – be it dispute resolution, intellectual property (IP) transactions, restructuring and insolvency or banking, financial and commercial transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is therefore important for Singapore to continue to build a strong legal framework that is business-minded and forward-looking; develop first-class legal services and jurisprudence; and really be at the forefront of legal thought leadership.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And all these will strengthen our value proposition as a global business centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, legal and IP sectors are also growth engines in and of themselves, contributing to the economy and jobs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our legal services sector has grown steadily over the years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are today amongst the most preferred arbitration seats in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) administers many cases which do not have a connection directly to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) also has an increasing caseload.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, last year, it had its most number of cases since it started operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But as Mr Murali says, we should not rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, we cannot because we are facing a challenging and competitive external environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If we do not continually improve, others will come in, fill the gap and take our space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we need to continue strengthening our legal hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our approach is a very practical one – to ensure that parties' commercial needs are met and we ensure party autonomy as far as possible, whether in the choice of law; choice of forum for dispute resolution, be it mediation, arbitration or the Singapore courts, including SICC; as well as the choice of counsel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also plugged in to the latest trends and developments, so that we can quickly move to update our laws and it moves in tandem with evolving mercantile needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we introduced various enhancements in international arbitration, which Mr Zhulkarnain mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2020, we provided a default mode of appointment of arbitrators in multi-party arbitration and recognised that the arbitral tribunal and the High Court have the power to enforce confidentiality obligations amongst the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2017 and 2022, we introduced additional funding options that were available in some other international arbitration centres, such as third-party funding and conditional fee agreements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, the Singapore Convention on Mediation (SCM) also mentioned by Mr Zhulkarnain, provides a uniform and efficient framework for parties to enforce their mediated settlement agreements across borders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have been actively encouraging countries to adopt the SCM and to promote mediation, through events and trainings, some of which, we do overseas as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we do this because, as the number of Convention Parties grow, mediation will also become more attractive for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore parties who trade with parties from any other Convention country, will be able to effectively use mediation as a means to resolve their disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can translate into time and cost savings, not to mention the preservation of goodwill and relationship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also involved in shaping international instruments, which may impact or potentially benefit Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw participated in the negotiations from 2015 until its completion in 2019, because we recognised its potential to increase enforceability overseas of Singapore judgments in commercial or civil matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Murali Pillai's specific query, we are now assessing whether to sign on and on what terms we will do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Along with a good legal framework, we need a robust, strong legal profession to serve businesses – law firms and lawyers, who can be trusted advisors to help businesses navigate different legal systems.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this, we aim to anchor top international law firms to strengthen our foreign and international law offerings; as well as continue to maintain a strong core of Singapore law practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am heartened to see Singapore law practices expanding their presence and networks overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I mentioned at the outset, Singapore is a small market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we need to view the region as our hinterland.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: ASEAN alone has a population of about 660 million and fast growing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And both these regions are the beneficiaries of increasing foreign direct investments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, MinLaw is committed to supporting our law firms in their internationalisation efforts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We received feedback that this helped them to better understand the Singapore legal market and form new connections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in turn, our Singapore lawyers through interaction with the Chinese lawyers, also understand the Chinese legal market better.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This programme will help them also build networks, understand the nuances of doing business in a foreign jurisdiction and strengthen their value proposition as a lawyer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If there is demand, we will explore similar programmes with other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Raj Joshua Thomas highlighted a moment ago, they are an important part for our legal ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many of our small firms have deep expertise in niche areas and some of them take on international, high-value work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, most of the Singapore lawyers who are going on this Shanghai exchange that I spoke about, come from smaller firms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Thomas also asked how we can support small firms, joining practices together to form a larger entity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Small Singapore practices can come together to form Singapore group practices with other freestanding law practices now, if they wish.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This enables firms to reach broader, allow them to reap benefits of co-branding, reap economies of scale in office as well as resource costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides law firms, we are also look at developing our lawyers – from the time they enter law school, right through to when they go into practice and beyond.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last month, the Working Group for the Reform of Legal Education made recommendations on legal education and training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Essentially, to keep pace with developments and shifts in other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One recommendation was to enhance the coverage of civil law concepts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We see this as an important area, because more than half of Singapore's top trading partners operate in civil law jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Earlier, we also accepted the Committee for the Professional Training of Lawyers' recommendations aimed at lifting overall standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked about the readiness of the firms and students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, Ms Samdin would recall that we announced this in 2018, some six years ago, precisely to give sufficient lead time to trainees and firms to make that transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was to have come into effect last year, but we deferred it by one year, taking into account the impact of COVID-19, as well as industry feedback.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes, overall, will help our lawyers better meet the challenges of competition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, as we all know, learning should not stop, even after one is called to the Bar and out in practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Legal practice is always evolving, as the world keeps moving and commercial needs keep evolving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong emphasised in his Budget speech, we also need to equip our workers for life, likewise lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides broad-based support, MinLaw has also introduced specific, targeted support for the legal industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, Ms Nadia Samdin would be pleased to know that we have introduced a secondment programme for young lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These secondments seek to provide young lawyers with exposure to high-growth areas in our economy, such as block-chain technology, as well as international sustainability financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows our lawyers to deepen industry knowledge and skillsets, also build contacts and networks with the relevant industry path makers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we will do our best to create opportunities for young lawyers, but they will need to also step up to seize these opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Indeed, Ms Nadia Samdin spoke about the challenges faced by young lawyers, including the intensified pace of work that they experience today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is feedback that we have heard in our regular engagements with young lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those of us who are lawyers in this Chamber were once young lawyers, maybe some are still young lawyers, we know that sometimes, practice can be challenging, clients are demanding, hours are long.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we should collectively do our best to improve the work culture, allow for more mentoring of young lawyers, guide them in the profession, expose them to opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we also have to recognise the reality that we have to live with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We live in a globalised world today, I spoke about the competition earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are competing with not just the lawyers within Singapore, but also from overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If we are not careful, we will lose our competitive edge and lose work and our market share to other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fundamentally though, I think our young lawyers are resilient, very forward looking, very determined to do well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, on our part, we will continue to enhance our legal industry and seek out opportunities for young lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These efforts, overall, will also deepen the strength of our legal industry, which Mr Murali Pillai highlighted, and ensure that Singapore continues to be a strong legal hub, one that encourages businesses, including MNCs, to choose Singapore for their operations and meet their legal needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Generative artificial intelligence, or GenAI, has received attention recently, some good, some not so good.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to encourage law practices to embrace technology to help them level up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will know that we introduced the Legal Technology Platform (LTP) for lawyers previously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, document review and assembly tools can drastically cut down the time needed for some rote tasks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Lawyers can then be freed up to do higher-value work, or client-facing work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the IDP is designed to work in tandem with the LTP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also looking to include tools in our current grant, the Productivity Solution Grant for the Legal Sector, to help Singapore law firms level up on the technology front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The value of an enterprise now increasingly lies in IP and intangible assets, or IA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can be seen from the increase in IP filings globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is, thus, important for us to continue to maintain a strong regime that is business-friendly and very forward-looking as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In recent years, we have updated our laws to keep pace with developments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2021, we overhauled the Copyright Act, in light of new technologies and also market developments in the digital age.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2022, we made amendments to improve the IP registration processes, made it more business-friendly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our Courts have also contributed with important jurisprudence, such as the I-Admin decision that changed the law on breach of confidence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But having a strong network and protecting IP is really just the beginning for us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What will add value to a business is the ability to commercialise and monetise their IP, and use it as a stepping stone to grow their businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIPS 2030 is designed to help enterprises unlock the value of their IA and their IP; spur innovation in the economy, as Mr de Souza said; and also support overall economic growth, particularly for the small and medium enterprises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will better support businesses in their IP journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And let me give Members some examples of the programmes that the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) has.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Last September, IPOS launched GoBusiness IP Grow, an online platform with a wealth of IP resources, including free tools, guides, programmes, as well as access to Government grants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This adds to existing programmes, such as the IP Business, as well as the Legal Clinics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IP is also important for youths, budding entrepreneurs and arts creators, as Ms Nadia Samdin mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To increase awareness, IPOS has a wide range of resources on various platforms made available and it constantly refreshes and updates them in response to market trends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, we have the recent AskTheExpert video series on copyright and trademark matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS also works with industry partners to support microbusinesses, as well as freelancers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And often it is this segment of society or the economy, who are not able to unlock the value in their own IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, IPOS, for example, has worked with the National Library Board and the Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association Singapore, and we held a session recently for creators to come together, and learn from IPOS on how to better protect their works with IP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This helps them level up, monetise and go further.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I mentioned, it is also critical to support growing businesses with more sophisticated IP strategies and management processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This pairs local businesses with experts, coming together to develop IP strategies in a curated way, institutionalise IP management processes, and also, overall, help to build IP capacity to sustain business growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IP Ready will support the development of key innovation sectors, such as the information and communications technology (ICT) as well as the biomedical technology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also support businesses in monetising the value of IP and other intangible assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also working on guidelines for valuing these IA, so that there is a common platform and a common standard and then, that value and the way that you use the value to monetise, can be interoperable across different markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Together, these initiatives will help businesses and investors appreciate and leverage on the true value of a business' IA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also important that we tackle community disputes quickly, before the disputes become intractable, causing irreparable rifts in society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This rift could then lead to neighbourly friction and ultimately, loosen the threads in the fabric of our cohesion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members know, we have been working on a revised framework to address this issue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One, the Ministry of National Development (MND) has been stepping up efforts to promote and encourage, as well as enforce pro-social norms upstream and will also set up a dedicated team of personnel to respond on the ground, something I will come back to in a moment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And third, where parties end up at the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRT), we want to enhance the processes and the powers of the CDRT to make it a far more expedient and efficient process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are parties who will continue to have to live side by side and probably see each other every day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, rather than look at a legal right or legal wrong in a vacuum, mediation helps to bring parties together, look at the bigger picture, look at the overall relationship, and come to reach an understanding and compromise on the matter far more easily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This also helps to keep the parties on good terms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Today, we have close to 160 volunteer mediators and we will continue to grow this pool.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CMC has also set up satellite mediation venues in the neighbourhoods, so that residents can take part in mediation closer to their homes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CMC has also started using Zoom for mediation, in the appropriate cases, to make mediation even more accessible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is in line with the suggestion that some Members have spoken about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the dedicated response team that I mentioned earlier will be given powers to come onto the ground, understand the problem, triage and identify suitable cases, and direct the neighbours to go to mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In many community disputes cases, quick intervention can often help to prevent the matter from escalating further, before emotions set in and parties become intractable in their positions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, apart from mandating parties to attend mediation, this team will also, in the appropriate cases, be present on site at the location of the disamenity and will be empowered to issue warnings and advisories.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Non-compliance with an abatement order will be an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are now preparing to set up this dedicated team of officers, which will take some time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But for a start, we intend for this unit to cover community disamenities, like noise and hoarding, which could have a serious impact on community harmony.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, going to the CDRT should really be a measure of last resort, only if all the other upstream intervention measures that I spoke about do not yield a successful outcome.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But for those who have to turn to the CDRT, it probably means you have gone through a process, you are unable to resolve it and it has been an issue for some time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We want to turn the CDRT process into: one, that allows parties to obtain relief quickly and effectively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have, therefore been working closely with the CDRT to identify several process areas which we will improve.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will allow affected residents to obtain quick relief, even as the case awaits a full hearing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This framework has been the subject of public consultations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On these ideas, generally the responses have been positive and supportive, and we will take onboard this feedback, make some adjustments as may be appropriate, and frame the legislation, because these measures will require legislative support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we are targeting to introduce this later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further details will be shared in due course.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Chairman, the last key thrust of MinLaw’s work relates to state assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Singapore Land Authority (SLA) plays a key role as custodian of state land and property, optimising land resources for our economic and social development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We continue to plan for the long term, to optimise our limited land and invest in our shared tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how SLA optimises state assets to meet market needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA remains continually attuned to market needs through extensive engagements, in order to unlock the value of state land and properties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also recognise that spaces play an important role in forging social cohesion and promoting social good in our community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA has been repurposing spaces to serve the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This space will be a collective impact hub that houses social purpose organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Foundry was set up in partnership with The Majurity Trust, Tote Board and the recently launched Singapore Government Partnership Office, and will facilitate the gathering of non-profit startups and social sector partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Bringing these partners together in a common space will create strong synergies to encourage civic participation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It will act as a base for non-profit organisations and social sector enablers to come together to incubate ideas, drive impactful innovation and build communities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are seeking innovative ideas for facilities and programming that will appeal to residents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On Ms Usha Chandradas’ comment relating to use by arts groups, SLA works with our partner agencies to identify suitable properties for arts uses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In general, SLA will consider factors such as market demand for the specific use, as well as feedback from community and stakeholders, including partner agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The rental of state properties to arts tenants will be based on the assessed market rate for such arts-related uses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about SLA’s management of state land and properties, in particular heritage bungalows.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Leong and Mr Patrick Tay also asked about the occupancy rates of state properties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of the points raised by Mr Leong were already addressed in Parliament last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The occupancy rates for residential heritage bungalows from January 2017 to January 2023 were shared publicly last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, the overall occupancy rate for usable state properties is published annually.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is publicly available information published in MOF’s Budget Book.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, the Member’s statements relate to the remaining 1%.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Occupancy rates of state properties generally move in tandem with changes in market conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When market conditions are weak and the demand for leasing is low, occupancy rates will generally be lower, as was the case for the Ridout Road estate in 2018, when a number of bungalows in that and other estates were vacant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, for heritage bungalows in particular, the pool of potential tenants is limited, because tenants often have to put in considerable additional work to install modern amenities to make the property more liveable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA’s approach is to make basic additions to ensure that the properties are in a reasonably good condition so that tenants are able to reside in these properties safely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The incoming tenant will also retrofit and enhance the property based on their preferences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since the tenant will have to spend a fair bit of money, that reduces the pool of tenants further.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA will install modern amenities and facilities for selected properties, where the overall circumstances make it advantageous to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have and will continue to rejuvenate properties, with an external private sector partner where possible to place-make the area.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It would, however, not be the best use of public resources to always renovate properties to a high standard before a tenant is found.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is because the condition of the property will deteriorate if there is no take-up such as in a poor market.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Taxpayers' money would have to be used again, to redo some works and carry out additional works, when a tenant is found.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is also wasteful and inefficient if we retrofit a property in a particular way only for the tenant to redo it in a different way.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It was also explained in detail that SLA deploys state properties to a variety of different uses.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Likewise, the surrounding state land is used in a variety of ways, having regard to the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) Master Plan.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While we continue to retain heritage bungalows for their original residential use on the market, some have been demolished as a cluster to make way for newer developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Others have been re-purposed for different uses, such as commercial and retail.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are subject to the URA Master Plans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If the heritage bungalows are located amidst or amongst an area zoned for landed properties, removing the properties or redeveloping them and the land around them would not change the area much.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The cleared land can only be similarly used for low intensity development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It should be kept in mind that SLA’s portfolio of state properties cannot be directly compared to that of a typical private commercial landlord, as SLA manages a number of heritage bungalows which are conserved or marked for study for conservation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA has carefully broadened the usage and deployment of its properties to meet the evolving needs of Singapore over time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A judicious balance continues to be needed, between protecting heritage properties in Singapore and redeveloping them altogether.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: SLA diversifies the management of its portfolio to include private sector managing agents as they are professional organisations, experienced in managing properties in the public and private markets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Building on the first Geospatial Master Plan, this will guide our national geospatial initiatives over the next decade.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, to mainstream geospatial information and technology to benefit Singaporeans in their daily lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will help make Singapore a more inclusive society for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, to deepen Singapore’s geospatial capabilities to support national needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This supports strategic use cases, such as urban planning, national security, coastal protection and flood mitigation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To address Ms Nadia Samdin’s query on harnessing AI, SLA launched the OneMap GPT Challenge with IMDA in October 2023.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This explored the usage of GenAI technology to enhance OneMap’s usefulness and relevance to the daily lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Third, to project Singapore’s leadership in geospatial development globally.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since 2022, SLA has been co-chairing the UN Expert Group on Land Administration and Management.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a strong recognition of Singapore’s achievements in maintaining a robust framework and mapping technology for land registration and ownership management.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have been sharing our experience and contributing to the global shift towards using geospatial information and technologies to address climate change challenges, such as coastal protection and flood mitigation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I turn now to speak about strengthening our criminal justice system, a point which Mr Patrick Tay had asked about.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Earlier this month, Parliament passed the Criminal Procedure Code (Miscellaneous Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The amendments were significant and focused on: protecting the public by strengthening our levers to tackle crime, including serious sexual crime; and enhancing transparency, fairness and coherence in our criminal court processes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Key amendments included: setting out a clear legislative framework on the conduct of forensic medical examinations; the introduction of a new sentence for enhanced public protection to better protect the public from dangerous offenders; and the introduction of new provisions on criminal disclosure to provide greater clarity, certainty and coherence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together, these amendments will facilitate more effective criminal investigations, enhance public protection and result in greater transparency and fairness in criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Separately, the inter-agency Sentencing Advisory Panel, which MinLaw is represented on, alongside stakeholders such as the Courts, the Attorney-General's Chambers, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Public Defender's Office and the Defence Bar, issued its first Guidelines on Reduction in Sentences for Guilty Pleas in August last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Guidelines provide more clarity, consistency and transparency to existing sentencing practice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They are intended to encourage accused persons who wish to plead guilty to do so earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This has significant benefits, especially for victims, as they can find closure sooner and are spared the need to testify in court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, for our civil legal aid scheme and criminal defence aid scheme, we will be revising the quantum of eligibility thresholds for per capita household income (PCHI) and annual value (AV).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is in light of the increase in household income and property value in recent years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The AV threshold for both types of aid will also be increased from $13,000 to $21,000, in line with MOF’s revision of the AV threshold for social assistance schemes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will cover all Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are working towards implementing these changes by the second quarter of this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On a related note, Mr Derrick Goh had asked whether exceptions are being considered for those who do not meet the means test criteria.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to exercise flexibility for deserving cases.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For instance, a Means Test Panel appointed by the Minister can consider and recommend aid be granted to applicants who cannot afford basic legal services due to extenuating circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Next, we are simplifying the application process for divorce matters in the Syariah Court.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This can help applicants minimise form-filling errors, and be better informed of their rights and entitlements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are looking to translate the tool into the Malay language in the next phase of development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is related to the point that our services need to be accessible to non-English speakers, which was also mentioned by Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When an applicant approaches MinLaw for services, we will try to find officers who speak the applicant’s preferred language to assist the applicant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: If this is not possible, we will find other ways to get translation done.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MinLaw also has non-English versions of brochures relating to some of our services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, MinLaw is also looking at making it easier for litigants to enforce their judgments, as said by Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have received feedback that sometimes, the time and costs spent to enforce judgments may be disproportionate to the outcome.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It may simply not be worth the effort to seek enforcement of lower-value judgments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One of the issues is that the current civil enforcement process is overly reliant on the compliance and cooperation of the judgment debtors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Under the Rules of Court, the current process to locate and identify a judgment debtor’s assets is for the judgment debtor to be examined in Court on his or her assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, the effectiveness of this procedure is dependent on the truthfulness and cooperation of the judgment debtor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An uncooperative judgment debtor could provide selective or insufficient information, or wear down the judgment creditor by failing to turn up for hearings or bring the required documents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are thus studying potential enhancements, such as giving the Court greater powers to identify the assets and means of judgment debtors, to help the judgment creditor decide whether and how to enforce the judgment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also looking to introduce new powers to deter and punish non-compliance with court orders and to streamline further the process of civil enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Vikram Nair had asked about the status of these proposed reforms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Another area which MinLaw and the FJC have been working on is probate and intestacy matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In response to Mr Murali Pillai on the potential expansion of its scope, the FJC will monitor its use first, as the e-Service was only introduced recently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On other possible areas for law reforms, I thank Mr Murali Pillai for his suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Given the full slate of work outlined earlier, which MinLaw is committed to delivering, some of these reviews will have a longer tail.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, my clarifications concern the Family Justice Reform's MEP component which Minister shared earlier that it will rolled out in stages.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I wish to find out what will be the Ministry's efforts when the MEP is being rolled out in stages to ensure that there is sufficient awareness on the ground, particularly the litigant-in-person, to make sure that they know where to seek help and what will be the procedures in line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lawyers will be expected to know the Act, the provisions, the powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will be expected to talk to the litigant-in-person and this is one process that is available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, through both the legal process as well as physically in the Courts, the information will be available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to do more of that.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I just wanted to clarify on my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think I said 580 cases out of 1,300 were ineligible.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister mentioned that there were about 440 cases that were handled by PDO and by CLAS as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What criteria does CLAS use and will the threshold changes apply to how CLAS assesses whether it should be giving aid as well?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And CLAS has its own set of criteria.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a clarification for Senior Parliamentary Secretary Ms Rahayu Mahzam on the access for non-English speakers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier on, she mentioned that there are brochures in different languages and indeed, it is true for some of the departments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what I noted that was also very good that MinLaw did was that for the Community Mediation Centres, there are videos in different languages which are also narrated in the different languages and subtitled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, this is very useful for our older residents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was hoping that MinLaw could also consider having videos in other aspects of community legal services so that we can direct our residents to watch them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I declare I am a lawyer in private practice and part of my practice encompasses IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think in order for us to become a solid IP hub, we need to ramp up our ability to value intangible assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If I may be permitted just to give an example.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most of the cases that go to Court are trademark infringement, patent infringement, copyright infringement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And then, assuming the plaintiff wins, he has got a judgment saying that his patent has been infringed, there is actually a dearth of case law on how to value that infringement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a dearth of case law globally, regionally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we want to become an IP hub, what we really need, in my humble view, is to increase our ability to monetise and value that IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nowadays, so much of what companies' asset is, is in intellectual property; it is not in the building, it is not in the bricks and mortar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is in the trade secrets, it is in the confidential information.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to know, in order to advance Singapore's position as an IP hub, what are we doing to bolster our valuation of IP capability and thereby attracting people here to dispute their IP, to protect their IP and to advance their IP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you take the Standard and Poor's 500 list of companies as an example, over the last five, 10, 15 years, a growing number of those companies reported that the majority of their assets are in intangible assets, no longer brick and mortar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think we have to be ahead of the curve if we want to be an IP hub that is of value to the business community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In valuation, what is important is you must have a clear, objectively assessed and accepted standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we can do that, then, we will begin to build on that body of case law that Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned, because then, you will have cases that deal with transactions of intangible assets and how they are valued.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You then have industry experts coming forward to give expert evidence on how to value intangible assets, in the same way as we now have industry experts who can quite easily value property and other types of assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is the trajectory that we are on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not something we can jump forward ahead by ourselves because what we do and how we do it has necessarily got to be done in tandem with other jurisdictions and other markets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They are trying to go into valuation of intangible assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I acknowledge the work of IPOS and its ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But if we can steal the march, as it were, if we can be ahead of the curve in different regions, then, this can really be an asset valuation hub and give that fillip and advantage to Singapore being an IP hub.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I want to assure the Member that that indeed is our aspiration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We do want to be ahead of the curve and that is why we have set up the framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have set up our working committee amongst the different Ministries, working with industry professionals and experts from around the world, precisely to do that.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, I would like to thank Minister Edwin Tong for hearing and acknowledging some of the stresses faced by young lawyers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would just like to go back to the clarification which I sought.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that the Ministry has decided that we are not going to prescribe a minimum quantum in terms of the honorarium which trainees will receive during this lengthened training period, but that the Ministry as well as Law Society was looking into granting leave days and medical leave to support trainees during this extended one-year period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these are options for young lawyers whilst at training to level up and to be supported on their journey of learning as they seek to qualify and get called to the Bar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the Member has other suggestions, as she often does, we are very happy to work with her, bring them on board and also work with the Law Society to ensure that our young lawyers benefit from these programmes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three questions for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First question, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that the rental income from the state properties far exceed the maintenance cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second question, what are the various plans under study now to manage the black and white bungalows to generate a higher return for the Government and, in turn, for the taxpayers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How is the Ministry going to publicise these plans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because the feeling is that currently, there is not much publicity on the heritage properties and how to invite more Singaporeans or investors to come and suggest ideas to better the performance on these bungalows.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third question, as an overall strategy, is there a review on whether there is a need to preserve so many black and white bungalows for heritage purposes?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Chairman, I would just like to give a few responses to address Mr Leong Mun Wai's questions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Suffice to say that the key thing is this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There were assertions Mr Leong made about the management of SLA in respect of these properties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have also specified and explained quite rigorously and I have also repeated that in the bulk of my speech to explain how efforts are being taken in managing this, in making sure that we do not necessarily overspend or waste resources.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think this actually shows how we have taken great efforts in managing the assets and, as you can see, the figures that I have also given, a large percentage of them are occupied.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And we have indicated that the rental that is received far exceeds the maintenance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Leong had also suggested that, perhaps, there is not enough publicity or information about the efforts that SLA is doing in managing state assets and optimising the resources we have.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I actually spent a bulk of my speech explaining all the different uses and the different efforts we are taking with different partners.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think that goes to show that there is a lot of thought put into it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It also ties in with the last question he raised about the overall strategy in deciding what to keep, what not to keep.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have also mentioned that in my speech because it is looking at the overall portfolio and deciding what are the best measures to take in light of the uses that are relevant at that time and in light of the partners that we are working with.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, I believe a lot of this has already been addressed in my speech and I just want to re-assert the point that SLA takes a lot of effort in looking at the overall market, the overall demands of the nation in the decisions they make in the management of these.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have two clarifications for Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And if that is the case, would SLA be open to reconsidering this position, given the important role that arts groups play in place-making in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note the Member's concern in this space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, the feedback that you have raised and the concerns that she has raised, I would have to take it back to the different agencies and we can see what other support can be provided.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Edwin Tong, do you want to add to that?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I thought I would jump in because if we do not answer it now, you might ask me during the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) COS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I thought I might as well deal with it now.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it gives a subsidy at the central level, not through SLA because it comes through NAC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And when NAC is of the view that this company or this artist adds value in terms of the field of art or is able to place-make, amongst other considerations, it then decides on subventing the particular group or groups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is how the arts companies and artists get their subvention – not directly from SLA but through NAC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Chairman, I agree with the Senior Parliamentary Secretary that since the Ministerial Statement last year on Ridout Road, a lot more information has emerged about the black and white bungalows.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But that does not mean that there is no further information that Singaporeans would like to know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, these are questions that Singaporeans would like to know and if enough information is being given, then we can assess better whether we have a big underutilised asset here or not.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note that the Member is really quite pre-occupied with the details and the specifics, and he has repeatedly asked these questions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But I think the point we are making is this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: At the end of the day, what is the larger point that is being made?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And our concern is the larger assertion that is being made that there is mismanagement, that SLA is not doing its part in ensuring that there is proper utilisation, optimisation of the state assets, state properties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That is something that is more important for us to debunk.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The truth is we have given a lot of other facts to show that the market dictates some points like the occupancy rates, vacancy rates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: All these are things that we have already highlighted to Mr Leong.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have also explained what are the considerations that SLA takes into account in deciding what to do with the different portfolios, the different state assets and state properties that it has in its bucket.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think there is a distinction between just vulgar curiosity and actually what are the assertions that are being made on this front.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And I am really concerned because I think at the end of the day, it has been repeated many times that SLA has not been looking at this thoroughly, has not been managing this well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think that is something that is most important for us to address.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Which is why I have repeatedly explained that the assets have been managed, we have explained how SLA does this, what SLA takes into account in dealing with these matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And I think it is important for us to understand and reiterate the point that there is optimisation, there is proper management of the state assets and state properties.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, for any further clarifications, please keep it short.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Chairman, I just want to make one point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It may not be a clarification in the strict definition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we did not start off stating that SLA has mismanaged the properties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
