text: A lot of things have been said, but there are still many questions that are unanswered.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We did not start off saying that SLA has mismanaged this or mismanaged that, but we are saying that there are questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if you can provide the answers, then you will be able to erase the doubts in the minds of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will take note of Mr Leong's suggestions, but I do want to also highlight that in your speech you did indicate that there were areas that SLA could look into in improving and you did say that it could do better, suggesting that there were some gaps in the things that have been done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, that is where I draw reference from.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But I do note that things constantly evolve, there may be developments and there may be updates that we can give.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, over time, that is something that we are prepared to do and provide information that is relevant to address concerns that Singaporeans and yourself may have.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Usha Chandradas, did you raise your hand earlier?

speaker: The Chairman
text: I think we have time for one more clarification.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: I just wanted to clarify that I am well aware of NAC's very, very good initiatives on arts housing, but what I have heard from artists on the ground is that demand for these schemes far exceeds the supply.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: So, the reason why I was raising this query through a cut for MinLaw was to see whether SLA could expand the scope of what it does and consider extending some subsidies to arts groups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is one of the challenges we face, not just in the arts sector, but really across a number of different sectors, including the sports sector.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What we do through the scheme is to best optimise it, to understand the needs of the landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, we do not just give the land or the arts spaces to established companies for long periods of time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We try and ensure that there is a turnover so that newer, nascent arts companies in emerging areas, developing areas of artworks can have an opportunity to be in these spaces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is how we manage it through NAC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would also add to Ms Usha's point that we do from time to time try to expand the number of spaces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because it does show that there is a growing arts ecosystem and people are interested: people want to make art a way of life and they want to be able to work, perform as well as exhibit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All these bode well for our overall arts ecosystem, which I am sure, no doubt, we will discuss more of next week.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can I invite Mr Murali, if you would like, to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It deals with high policies, dealing with the internationalisation of Singapore, maintaining our status as a legal hub and so on, and at the same time, it focuses on the small man.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The poignant example given by the hon Minister about how the PDO helped a gentleman named Mr N to get an equitable sentence is very heartwarming indeed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Also, the processes outlined by the hon Second Minister on how to maintain peace in the community – something all hon Members can ascribe to.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Last but not least, the processes to allow the common man navigate the courts better, as outlined by the hon Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, Sir, I seek leave to withdraw my amendment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg leave to move "that the total sum to be allocated for Head R of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our strong legal system and our deep commitment to the rule of law are key contributors to our country's business friendly environment and have made us a leading international legal services hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Ministry of Law (MinLaw) continues to be heavily involved in building up our capacity to be a global hub for intellectual property (IP) activities too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore's legal industry continues to attract top notch talent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, however, getting more and more difficult to maintain our position.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Several jurisdictions are investing significant resources to develop their own capabilities to be business friendly and to attract legal work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What are MinLaw's plans to ensure that we keep up with the competition?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area I am particularly interested is how we can deepen the bench strength of Singaporean and Singapore-based arbitrators so that they more regularly feature in high value arbitrations conducted by institutions such as the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) and the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), in addition to the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We can also be more tightly woven into the global legal system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will strengthen the ability of Singapore judgments to be recognised and enforced in the European Union.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One other suggestion I have is to consider reforms to allow for execution of electronic deeds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deeds are the lifeblood of so many commercial transactions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many security documents such as charges are executed as deeds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In countries with financial centres such as the United Kingdom (UK), formalities such as the need to execute in wet ink have been done away with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not yet the case in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore needs to secure its position in the global legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, it needs to ensure that laws serve to secure justice for everyone in our community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MinLaw has made great strides over the years to improve access to justice, particularly for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There has been excellent utilisation of technology to offer laypeople with easier and cost-effective means to get advice on standard cases, commence action in tribunals and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am particularly pleased with the launch of the Probate eService last year which will enable self-represented persons to apply for probate – something that I have been pushing for several years now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The process now is simpler, faster and much cheaper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I commend the team responsible for the successful launch of this e service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether there are plans to scale up the eService offerings in the near future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, the e-services apply to probate matters involving sole executors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to look at providing similar services to intestacy matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This convention assists testators to dispose of inheritance within a single will, even if the property in question may be situated in different countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I raise this not to trivialise the amount of work that has to be put into the review of these matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am also aware of the heavy legislative agenda of MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is just that the cases have been made for law reform in these areas for some time now and are based, amongst others, on possible unfairness that will fall on individuals should the current status quo persists.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, geospatial data can help us better understand Singapore at different points in time, influencing urban planning decisions and actions to even tackle climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Diverse technologies have erupted and are at various stages of maturity, some of which could significantly improve land planning processes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include geospatial innovations such as scanning technologies, metaverse developments and various forms of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) have to further develop and expand the use of geospatial data and technology?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does the SLA plan to encourage knowledge sharing and collaboration, possibly leveraging open technology to optimise the adoption and utilisation of these innovations for the benefit of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have state land and assets spread across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These should be optimised to support our economy and serve our country and community.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How many of these plots of state land and assets are disused or under-utilised and how is SLA optimising our state assets and making the best use possible of all these land and assets whilst meeting market needs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Are we also leveraging on technology, including geospatial capabilities to enhance the capabilities of SLA?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, last year Singaporeans learned about two of our Ministers who were renting large black and white bungalows sitting on hundreds of thousands of square feet of prime land from SLA for $20,000 to $30,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The subsequent debates on the issue make Singaporeans aware of a large under-utilised asset that forms part of our past reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My cut today will focus on some questions regarding how state lands, including black and white bungalows, are managed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SLA has a responsibility to judiciously manage these assets.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially important for cases where the lands are rented out for less than 10 years because in these cases the rents do not form part of the Past Reserves protected by the President.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we have little other information on the management of state lands and properties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not know the total cost of maintenance, for example.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also do not know how many of these properties are vacant and for how long.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that no landlord would allow this to happen with their properties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why did SLA and its managing agents allow this to happen?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Who are the managing agents and how are they appointed?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a situation should never have been allowed to happen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Government has been very careful to recover the market value of land, even if it is for public housing, it seems less concerned about the fact that state properties can be vacant, not generating any income and falling into disrepair for years, even if they are in prime and prestigious areas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) calls on SLA to reveal these statistics, not only for black and white bungalows, but for all state properties under its charge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rental values of many black-and-white bungalows are negatively impacted because they are not retrofitted to modern standards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Ms Hazel Poa asked Minister Edwin Tong, why SLA does not install modern amenities to improve demand and rental rates.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister's response was that modernisation could be carried out if SLA was able to cluster and rejuvenate these bungalows.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans would also like to know what is the total land area occupied by the 2,600 state properties and SLA should look into making better use of large land parcels that currently form part of the state properties.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These large land parcels are currently not attached to value, because it is market practice to use Gross Floor Area (GFA) as the guiding component in determining rents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are also considered "liabilities" to the tenants.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This House has a responsibility to ensure this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: State properties like black-and-white bungalows should generate good value for the taxpayer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under no circumstances should they be allowed to be under-utilised, fall into disrepair and be vacant for years.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, affordable arts housing is hard to find in Singapore and yet, the arts have a crucial role to play in placemaking or, in other words, the creation of meaningful spaces where people live, work and play.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to refer to academic Hoe Su Fern and her 2019 article entitled, "The role of the arts in placemaking Singapore".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: She says, "Every space has a history, a culture, and connections to the other spaces around it.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As idea-makers and story-tellers, artists are able to create unique, uplifting stories that inspire curiosity and a sense of discovery; and most crucially, build emotional connection to a place." This is especially relevant with regard to the older properties managed by SLA – which are full of local history, charm and interesting architectural detail.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Straits Times recently featured an article on the independent arts cluster located at 195 Pearl's Hill Terrace.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While arts offerings fulfill an important social aim and once again, this social aim was something that was identified by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in this very Budget.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These aims may not always be adequately supported by the operation of free market economics.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the Ministry is able to step in and assist with arts housing, it would not only alleviate the cost pressures faced by artists but it would also help to enliven these spaces around us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The issue of enforcement of judgments has always been a bugbear, including for the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) in the Labour Movement where we have obtained judgment for aggrieved workers at the Employment Claims Tribunal or State Courts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is so that a non-compliant judgment debtor cannot run away from his or her obligations so easily and that there can be greater powers to deter them from non-compliance of Court orders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will help in more ways than one to ensure that our civil justice system serves the needs of any aggrieved person who otherwise is left stuck and helpless.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   In my constituency, there are many elderly residents who are not proficient in English and they only understand Chinese, Malay and Tamil.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has indeed made some improvements in this regard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, translating the brochures of the Legal Aid Bureau and Public Defender’s Office into other official languages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, at last year's Committee of Supply debate, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam mentioned that MinLaw was considering possible reforms to the civil enforcement framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: She explained that the aim was to make enforcement cheaper and faster so that successful litigants can get the fruits of their litigation more quickly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The current tools available for civil enforcement have been around for decades – certainly longer than I have been in practice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These include orders to examine judgment debtors, to seize and sell assets and to garnish monies – say – in bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Typically, enforcement proceedings are separate from the main claim and need to be commenced separately.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With more information, the successful party can probably better decide whether and how to enforce the judgment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am particularly curious about what additional powers the Court and parties can tap to get information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For non-compliance with Court orders – where this would amount to contempt of Court – I would support stronger penalties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For simple non-compliance – say, of an order to pay damages, I would be more careful to introduce any additional penalties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is currently not a crime to be unable to pay a debt or a judgment debt; and impecuniosity itself should not be punished with imprisonment – other than usual consequences, such as bankruptcy and so on; are entirely legitimate if a debtor is unable to pay their debt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, there is also currently conduct that may be annoying but may not amount to contempt, such as delays in providing information or providing incomplete information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In these matters, it may be helpful to have some appropriate penalties in place to ensure timely compliance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Enforcement is an important matter for successful litigants.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be interested to know if there is any update by MinLaw on the review that it announced at the last Committee of Supply.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, I wish to first declare that I am a lawyer and my practice areas include family law.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the Opening of the Legal Year 2013, the hon Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon announced the establishment of the Committee for Family Justice, which was tasked to deliver recommendations on the new framework for the family justice system, including specifically on how distressed families may be better assisted in resolving their disputes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amongst other things, the recommendations sought to: one, further improve court proceedings and procedures in the Family Justice Courts; and two, enhance maintenance enforcement processes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Next, what were the challenges that were faced, along the way, to adopt the recommendations that were made since 10 years ago?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, how is the Ministry strengthening its ongoing efforts to ensure all relevant stakeholders are in sync and collaborating towards adopting and embracing Therapeutic Justice, which aims to help families in distress to heal and move on with their lives?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Over the years, this Government has demonstrated commitment to improve legal access for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: During the same time, applications to the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS), have fallen significantly.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This suggests that the PDO is playing an increasing role within our legal framework.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, can Minister provide an update on whether the PDO has met all its KPIs set out during its formation; and the challenges faced so far; as well as plans for further enhancements, along with the following three questions?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, whether the actual application rates are as expected and if the means test criteria are assessed to be appropriately set?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In respect of the means test, were any exceptions granted?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Second, given the complexity of each case that often includes non-legal aspects, whether the caseload per staff is manageable and if improvements are needed for closer partnerships with other agencies to address root causes of these vulnerable cases better?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And third, whether there have been successful cases of vulnerable applicants and their families receiving more holistic help in both the legal and non-legal areas?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Goh, you can move on to your next cut.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This means that for every month that passes, 4,000 households are unhappy with each other.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: The recent fatal case at Bukit Batok was reportedly due to a long-term neighbour dispute over noise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: This affirms how neighbour disputes must be managed early and effectively to avoid potentially severe consequences.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: But unfortunately, mediation remains voluntary and depends on the parties' willingness to attend such meetings.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Moreover, non-compliance with mediation agreements are still not effectively enforced.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Singapore's community dispute resolution mechanisms, hence, need to be urgently enhanced to increase its effectiveness in dealing with the increasing number of neighbour disputes that remain unresolved.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: I understand the initiative is still in progress.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Can Minister clarify the key steps taken so far and further measures to be taken, including legislation to be set in place to improve the effectiveness of community dispute management?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Can Minister also clarify the expected duration for the new unit to be operationalised, so that residents can seek effective relief?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Usually, it would be a complaint about noise, like the dragging of furniture, or loud footsteps on the floor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, it is about screaming children or quarrelling neighbours.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: On some occasions, abusive words would be used.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is extremely frustrating because there are no real solutions at this moment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We do not know whether the complainant is sensitive to noise or whether there are really such noises heard by the complainant late at night.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If there are such loud or irritating noises, it would be unbearable to try to sleep with such noise.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I had urged the Government to do more to address such neighbourly disputes because if the disputes are not dealt with quickly, then there would be anger and possibly violence against the other neighbour.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, many of us in this House will agree that one of the most challenging disputes to resolve in our work on the ground are those that involve neighbours within the community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In a land scarce Singapore, whether in the public or private estates, we mostly live in homes within a close community setting.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This has fostered strong relationships between neighbours and in the wider community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It has also strengthened our social compact, as neighbours of different races, cultures and religions live side by side in harmony.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I remember growing up in the corridors of our Joo Seng Estate in Potong Pasir.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I had many fond and fun memories of my childhood in Joo Seng.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I am not sure if my neighbours at that time felt the same way about me.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, once in a while, because of the close proximity that we live with one another, disputes between neighbours arise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In my experience, most of these disputes relate to noise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It could be noise between homes, or noise in the community during quiet hours.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These are disputes that are notoriously difficult to resolve.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Currently, we often ask our grassroots volunteers to step in and try and mediate between parties.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Sometimes, if the community can resolve its own disputes, the outcomes are often the most favourable.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If all else fails, then referral to a trained mediator at the CMC or, for more serious cases, to CDRT.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Outcomes often lack finality and does not effectively resolve the dispute.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One of the outcomes when disputes are not resolved, sometimes over years, is that one household may choose to sell their home and move away and during the sale, new buyers may unwittingly move in, completely unaware of the unresolved dispute.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In these cases, the new buyers may face the same issues as the previous owners and may even feel that they have been "conned" into purchasing their new home.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply, I remember hearing of plans by MinLaw to enhance the Community Dispute Resolution Framework.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There were plans for stronger laws, including mandating mediation and also to improve the CDRT process to give faster and more effective relief and piloting a team of dedicated personnel to facilitate dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister to share an update with this House on the enhancements that will be made to better facilitate the resolution of community disputes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you may take all your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, we live in a communitarian society, where we have to learn to live together and to do to others as we would have them do to us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That involves living with the occasional inconvenience, especially in Housing and Development Board (HDB) apartments where neighbours live side by side or in closely compact private property settings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But sometimes these inconveniences spill over into becoming an actual dispute and hence our need for the CDRT.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is one important way to allow neighbours to settle disputes in an amicable manner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has worked hard to build and maintain its social compact and strengthen harmonious bonds between heterogeneous groups and we should look to protect it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MinLaw share more details on how the enhancements that will be made to better facilitate the resolution of community disputes will happen?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, allow me to declare that I am a practising lawyer involved in areas such as IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has always held the firm belief in investing into IP infrastructure to support enterprises and the wider innovation community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can be seen through policies such as the 2013 IP Master Plan and Singapore IP Strategy 2030, which focus on building and IP ecosystem and enabling Singapore to become a global Asia note of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong IP regime is essential in encouraging our local enterprises and startups to be willing to push the frontiers of digital exploration and lead innovation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we want to have an innovation driven economy, we need to secure the rights of local businesses and individuals by allowing them to monetise their innovations and IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How has MinLaw been supporting the local enterprises in that effort, that is to monetise the intangible asset or the intellectual property in question?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This places us at the forefront of dispute resolution, not only in Southeast Asia, but even beyond.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are pro-business and we have the necessary infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have become a venue for IP and technology dispute resolutions and our Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) is world class.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we progress, what is MinLaw doing to continue to strengthen Singapore as a leading legal and dispute resolution hub, including supporting the legal profession and harnessing technology?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Chairman, I apologise for the interruption and I thank you for allowing me to have a chance to clarify.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: I forgot to declare my interest earlier when I was making my cut.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: In fact, I live in a property of which SLA is the landlord.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: So, I would like to declare my interest and I thank you for allowing me the chance to do that.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Which sectors does the Government currently target when undertaking company specific engagements to support enterprises, on other plans to expand the range of sectors in the coming years?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the IP Strategy also include guidance on how Creatives can manage and commercialise their IAIP assets, especially for younger creatives and small creative businesses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, may I move on to the next cut?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I continue to speak up for law students and young lawyers in this Chamber.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: It continues to be a challenging time for junior lawyers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Stiff competition and technology has driven an ever-intensifying piece of work in the profession.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Gen Y and Gen Z workforces each have different perspectives, such as on opportunities and kind of culture that they wish to see.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And I prepared to leave the profession for other opportunities if law firms do not evolve.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Last November, the House passed the Legal Profession amendment Bill, which is set to double the practise training period for trainee lawyers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: This has raised questions on trainee compensation and benefits, including leave days and medical leave.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: In line of strengthening Singapore's position as the leading International Legal Services Hub, does the Ministry have plans to create more opportunities for young lawyers to have secondment chances including to Southeast Asia or other parts of Asia?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Our SICC in the Supreme Court has also been attracting more international case filings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Its standalone set of procedural rules are a gamechanger in the international dispute resolution landscape.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: They provide expeditious and efficient administration of justice and procedural flexibility through fair, impartial and practical processes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This is important to parties facing the fast-changing needs and realities of international commerce.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this competitive global landscape, we must continue to strengthen Singapore's position as a leading international legal services hub and seize new opportunities and uphold our reputation as the preferred dispute resolution forum and also leverage on new ways to increase efficiency for the resolution of such disputes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Besides litigation and arbitration, our position straddles both the cultures of both east and west, which can help us play a part in the international mediation scene.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Can MinLaw update on the role of the Singapore Convention on Mediation and how that has helped the international mediation scene in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: What further improvements of the international arbitration framework can be expected to enhance our dispute resolution hub status?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The Conditional Fee Arrangements (CFAs) amendments have been extremely helpful in providing access to justice in arbitrations and other settings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In Singapore, CFAs offer an alternative fee structure, allowing individuals to pursue legal action without the burden of upfront costs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: By removing financial barriers, individuals who might have hesitated to pursue legal action due to costs, now can seek justice without fear of exorbitant fees.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This inclusivity enhances the fairness and equity within our legal system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Moreover, CFAs encourage lawyers to carefully assess the merits of a case before taking it on.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This not only improves the efficiency of the legal process but also contributes to the overall integrity of our system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore has implemented safeguards, to ensure that cases pursued under CFAs are grounded in legitimacy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Overall, this is good to increase access to justice for litigants and increase our attractiveness as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Recent amendments have also improved such access whether through legal aid for civil matters or the PDO or the CLAS for criminal matters.
